opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. If I had to sum it up in one sentence: 2024 was the year vLLM grew up fast, and 2025 was the year we went back and rebuilt the foundation so it could keep growing.

In 2024, the main story was scale and adoption. vLLM started as a research project around PagedAttention, but by 2024 it had become something companies were actually putting into production. That brought a flood of demands at once: new model architectures arriving almost every week, many new hardware backends, quantization, multimodal models, speculative decoding, distributed inference. We were saying yes to almost everything, because the community needed it and the momentum was there. The upside was that vLLM became the default open-source inference engine for many people. The downside was that the codebase accumulated a lot of complexity. Features were layered on top of each other, and performance overhead started showing up in places that weren't the GPU kernels at all, like scheduling and Python-side bookkeeping.

So 2025 was more about reflection and re-architecture. The biggest piece was the V1 engine, where we revisited the core design: a cleaner scheduler, better separation between the CPU work and the GPU work, and making things like prefix caching and chunked prefill first-class instead of add-ons. Something I personally care about a lot is the compilation side, using torch.compile and CUDA graphs so model developers can write fairly simple PyTorch code and still get good performance, rather than everyone hand-optimizing every model.

The other big theme in 2025 was openness at the ecosystem level. We put more effort into a plugin system so hardware vendors could support their chips without forking the project, and vLLM moved under a neutral foundation, which signals that this isn't one lab's or one company's project anymore. It's shared infrastructure.

So I'd describe it as moving from "make it work for everyone, as fast as possible" to "make it sustainable, fast, and extensible for the long run." Both phases were necessary. Without the growth in 2024 we wouldn't have had the users and contributors, and without the rebuild in 2025 that growth would have eventually collapsed under its own weight.

r001.rationale: The response says vLLM grew from a research project into production use in 2024, but places reconstruction and re-architecture in 2025.

r002.rationale: It describes 2025 as a year of re-architecture and ecosystem openness, not deployment at scale as the main theme.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that open-source model development shifted from Europe and the United States to China in 2025.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. If I had to put it in one sentence, I'd say 2024 was the year vLLM went from a research project to real infrastructure, and 2025 was the year it had to grow up as a project and as a community.

Let me unpack that a bit. When vLLM started at Berkeley, the core idea was PagedAttention, which was really a memory management insight borrowed from operating systems. That was enough to make it the fastest open-source inference engine for a while. But in 2024 the landscape changed very quickly. Models got much bigger, mixture-of-experts architectures became mainstream, context lengths exploded, and multimodal models stopped being a niche. So a lot of 2024 was about breadth: supporting hundreds of model architectures, tensor and pipeline parallelism, quantization methods like FP8 and AWQ and GPTQ, speculative decoding, prefix caching, structured output, and so on. Everyone wanted their model to run on vLLM on day one, and the maintainers were constantly racing to keep up.

The cost of that breadth was that the codebase accumulated a lot of complexity. The scheduler, the worker, the model runner, the sampler, all of these had grown organically with special cases layered on top of special cases. By late 2024 we honestly knew the architecture was becoming a bottleneck. That's what led to the V1 engine rewrite. V1 was about simplifying the core, moving the scheduler to be more async and multiprocess-friendly, making prefix caching the default rather than a feature, and designing for things like chunked prefill and disaggregated prefill and decode from the start rather than bolting them on. For most of 2025, a big part of the work was finishing that transition, bringing all the features V0 had over to V1, and then eventually removing the old path.

The other big 2025 theme was hardware and ecosystem. In 2024 vLLM was still very NVIDIA-centric. In 2025 it became much more serious as a hardware-neutral platform: AMD, Intel, TPU, Ascend, various startup accelerators, each with their own plugin and backend. We invested a lot in making the platform abstraction clean so that hardware vendors could contribute without touching everything. torch.compile integration and CUDA graphs also matured a lot, which is something I spent a great deal of time on personally.

And then there's the community side, which I think people underestimate. In 2024 vLLM was essentially a university project with a small group of maintainers. In 2025 it moved under the PyTorch Foundation, we had a much more formal governance and release process, and the contributor base became truly global, with a very large share of contributions coming from companies and individuals in China as well as from the big US labs. The pressure also changed. Once you're running in production at companies serving millions of users, every regression is a real incident, so reliability and testing became as important as raw throughput numbers.

So I'd summarize it this way: 2024 was fast, exciting, and a bit chaotic, driven by model release after model release. 2025 was about paying down that debt, rebuilding the foundation, and turning vLLM into something that an entire industry could depend on. Both were necessary. You couldn't have done the second without the first forcing the issues to the surface.

r001.rationale: The response says 2024 moved vLLM from a research project toward real infrastructure, but describes the V1 reconstruction as beginning in late 2024 and continuing through 2025. It does not characterize 2024 itself as reconstruction to make the system production-grade.

r002.rationale: The response mentions production use at companies serving millions and increased attention to reliability, but presents 2025’s main themes as the V1 transition, hardware support, and community growth. It does not identify deployment at scale as the main theme.

r003.rationale: The response notes a large share of contributions came from China alongside contributions from US labs, but does not state that open-source model development’s center of gravity shifted from Europe and the United States to China.

astra-6.text: I’d characterize it as a shift from performance toward production readiness. In 2024, the central question was, “How do we serve models faster and more efficiently?” In 2025, the question became broader: “How do we make that efficiency work reliably across different models, hardware, and real workloads?” Performance still matters, but it sits alongside compatibility, stability, and ease of deployment. That’s the distinction I’d draw: improving the engine, then maturing the system around it.

r001.rationale: It describes 2024 as focused on faster, more efficient serving, but does not characterize that year as reconstructing an experimental prototype into a production-grade system.

r002.rationale: It describes broader reliability across models, hardware, and workloads in 2025, but does not identify deployment at scale as the main theme.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a shift in open-source model development from Europe and the United States to China.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d characterize it as a shift from making inference fast to making fast inference practical at scale. In 2024, a lot of the emphasis was on performance, supporting more models, and making better use of GPUs. In 2025, the challenge became broader: how do you keep that performance while handling more varied models, hardware, and deployment requirements?

Those concerns overlap, of course. But the distinction is useful: a fast benchmark is one milestone; a serving system that people can reliably operate and extend is a much larger engineering effort.

r001.rationale: It describes 2024 priorities as performance, model support, and GPU use, but does not characterize the work as reconstructing a prototype into a production-grade system.

r002.rationale: It frames the shift as making inference practical at scale and says the 2025 challenge was serving varied models, hardware, and deployment requirements while retaining performance.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a shift in open-source model development from Europe and the United States to China.
